questions.q: A scenario needs data cleaned and reshaped with a low-code, transformation-first experience, with no need for pipeline orchestration of multiple activities. What's the better fit?
options: A deployment pipeline
A Data Factory pipeline
A Dataflow Gen2
A KQL database
questions.explain: Dataflow Gen2 is the transformation-first, low-code tool; Data Factory pipelines are for orchestrating multiple activities — matching the tool to what the scenario actually asks for.

questions.q: A team needs to aggregate streaming data into 5-minute windows inside a KQL database. Which KQL operator is built for this?
options: project, used alone
A OneLake shortcut
summarize, combined with a time-based bin
A deployment pipeline stage
questions.explain: summarize (paired with a time bin) is KQL's aggregation operator — project only reshapes columns, it doesn't aggregate.

questions.q: A 'Confidential' sensitivity label is applied to a Lakehouse table. A Spark notebook reads that table and writes a derived table from it. Should you assume the derived table is automatically protected with no further check?
options: The question is moot, because sensitivity labels don't apply to Spark notebooks
Yes — labels always disappear the moment data passes through a notebook
No — label inheritance to derived data depends on the governance configuration, so it needs to be verified rather than assumed
Yes — labels always apply with zero configuration required, in every case
questions.explain: This is a deliberately trickier governance twist: unlike the straightforward export case in Lesson 35, label propagation to derived data depends on the governance setup — an absolute assumption in either direction is the trap here.

questions.q: A contractor's project ends, but their workspace Contributor role was never removed. Which practice does this scenario point to?
options: Applying a sensitivity label to the contractor's account
Access reviews and least privilege — periodically checking for and removing access that's no longer needed
Setting up a deployment pipeline for the contractor
Enabling row-level security on every table the contractor touched
questions.explain: Fabric Lesson 63's access reviews and least-privilege practice directly targets this scenario: stale access from an ended engagement getting caught and removed.

questions.q: A pipeline change needs to reach production gradually, with the ability to roll back quickly if error rates spike. What deployment pattern fits?
options: The Monitoring Hub
A OneLake data access role
Blue-green or canary deployment
A sensitivity label
questions.explain: Blue-green/canary deployment (Fabric Lesson 65) is specifically the gradual-rollout-with-fast-rollback pattern — the other options don't address deployment risk at all.

questions.q: A pipeline is failing intermittently, and the team already knows it's failing (alerts are firing) but needs to understand exactly why. What's the correct next tool?
options: A deployment pipeline stage gate
The Monitoring Hub, since it already told them it's failing
A workspace role change
Observability — logs, metrics, and traces — to diagnose the root cause
questions.explain: Once you know something failed (via an alert or the Monitoring Hub), observability is the layer that explains why — a distinct job from either monitoring or deployment tooling.

questions.q: A system design trade-off question asks about choosing consistency over availability during a network partition. Which concept from this course's Chapter 1 does this connect to?
options: Blue-green deployment
OneLake shortcuts
Sensitivity labels
The CAP theorem
questions.explain: This connects back to Lesson 19's CAP theorem coverage — DP-700 scenario questions sometimes lean on system design fundamentals from earlier in this course, not just Fabric-specific features.

questions.q: A scenario names 'Eventhouse' as the ingestion component that pulls streaming data in from an external source. Is this correct?
options: Yes, Eventhouse and Eventstream are interchangeable names for the same feature
No — Eventstream is the ingestion component; Eventhouse (with its KQL database) is the storage/query destination
No, because neither Eventstream nor Eventhouse handles streaming data
Yes, Eventhouse always handles ingestion, and Eventstream is only for querying
questions.explain: This is the Eventstream/Eventhouse lookalike-item-type trap from Lesson 37: Eventstream ingests, Eventhouse (via its KQL database) stores and serves queries.

questions.q: A scenario describes a workload that fits comfortably on a small capacity SKU — but the final sentence adds that the org plans to onboard five more teams to the same capacity within the month. What does this qualifier change?
options: The capacity sizing decision — future combined load across all teams should be planned for, not just the current single workload
Nothing — the final sentence is irrelevant to the SKU decision
It means the workload must move to a Lakehouse instead of a Warehouse
It means a sensitivity label is now required
questions.explain: This is Lesson 37's buried-qualifier trap: the last clause changes the real question from 'does this fit now' to 'does this fit once five more teams share the same capacity.'
